title.zh: 卷九十三 列傳第六十三 外戚
title.raw: 卷九十三 列傳第六十三 外戚 Volume 93 Biographies 63: Imperial Affines

sentences.zh: 詳觀往誥，逖聽前聞，階緣外戚以致顯榮者，其所由來尚矣。

translations.literal: Carefully examining the admonitions of old and heeding what was heard in former times, those who climbed by ties to imperial affines to reach high honor—their origins go back a long way.
translations.idiomatic: A close reading of past injunctions and the lessons of earlier ages shows that riding kinship with the imperial consorts to wealth and rank is an old story.

sentences.zh: 而多至禍敗，鮮克令終者，何哉？

translations.literal: Yet many come to disaster and ruin, and few achieve a good end—why?
translations.idiomatic: Yet so many of them end in ruin, and precious few die in peace. Why is that?

sentences.zh: 豈不由祿以恩升，位非德舉；

translations.literal: Is it not because emolument rises through favor, and office is not raised up by virtue?
translations.idiomatic: Surely it is because their salaries come from imperial favor rather than merit, and their posts are not won by moral weight.

sentences.zh: 識慚明悊。

translations.literal: In insight they are ashamed before clear wisdom.
translations.idiomatic: Their judgment cannot bear comparison with true sagacity.

sentences.zh: 材謝經通；

translations.literal: In talent they decline short of mastery of the classics.
translations.idiomatic: Their abilities fall short of real command of the canon.

sentences.zh: 假椒房之寵靈，總軍國之樞要。

translations.literal: Borrowing the favor and numinous power of the harem, they grasp the pivot of both army and state.
translations.idiomatic: They lean on the consort’s favor to seize the levers of military and civil power.

sentences.zh: 或威權震主，或勢力傾朝；

translations.literal: Some awe the ruler with their might and authority; some tilt the whole court with their power and influence.
translations.idiomatic: Some overshadow the throne; others bend the entire bureaucracy to their will.

sentences.zh: 居安而不慮危，務進而不知退；

translations.literal: Dwelling in safety they do not think of peril; striving to advance they do not know to withdraw.
translations.idiomatic: They bask in ease and ignore danger; they press always forward and never learn when to step back.

sentences.zh: 驕奢既至，釁隙隨之者乎！

translations.literal: Once arrogance and extravagance have arrived, do breach and rift not follow!
translations.idiomatic: Arrogance and excess invite their own undoing—is that not how the cracks appear?

sentences.zh: 是以呂霍之家，誅夷于西漢，梁鄧之族，剿絕於東都，其餘干紀亂常、害時蠹政者，不可勝載。

translations.literal: Therefore the houses of Lü and Huo were exterminated in Western Han; the clans of Liang and Deng were cut off in the Eastern capital; as for the rest who violated the norm, threw order into chaos, harmed the age, and worm-eaten governance—they cannot all be recorded.
translations.idiomatic: Hence the Lü and Huo lines were slaughtered in Western Han, and the Liang and Deng families extirpated at Luoyang; the roll of affines who broke the law, subverted custom, and poisoned the state would fill volumes.

sentences.zh: 至若樊靡卿之父子，竇廣國之弟兄，陰興之守約戒奢，史丹之掩惡揚善，斯並后族之所美者也。

translations.literal: As for Fan Miqing’s father and son, Dou Guangguo’s brothers, Yin Xing’s keeping restraint and warning against extravagance, and Shi Dan’s covering evil and proclaiming good—these are what the empress’s kin have to praise.
translations.idiomatic: Then there are the shining exceptions: Fan Miqing and his father, Dou Guangguo and his brothers, Yin Xing with his frugality and discipline, Shi Dan who muted scandal and lifted virtue—all models among imperial in-laws.

sentences.zh: 由此觀之，干時縱溢者必以凶終，守道謙沖者永保貞吉，古人所謂禍福無門，惟人所召，此非其效歟！

translations.literal: Viewed from this, those who flaunt excess against the times surely end in ill fortune; those who keep the Way and are modest and yielding forever preserve steadfast good fortune. What the ancients called ‘fortune and disaster have no gate—only men summon them’—is this not its proof!
translations.idiomatic: From this it is plain: those who ride the moment to excess come to a bad end, while the modest who hold to the Way keep their good name. The old saying that we make our own fortune or ruin—here is the evidence.

sentences.zh: 逮于晉難，始自宮掖。

translations.literal: When it came to the Jin calamity, it began in the palace apartments.
translations.idiomatic: The Jin dynasty’s catastrophe began in the inner palace.

sentences.zh: 楊駿藉武帝之寵私，叨竊非據，賈謐乘惠皇之蒙昧，成此厲階，遂使悼后遇雲林之災，湣懷濫湖城之酷。

translations.literal: Yang Jun relied on Emperor Wu’s private favor and grasped what he should not have held; Jia Mi rode Emperor Hui’s dullness and made this stair of evil, so that Empress Dao met disaster at Yunlin, and Min Huai suffered cruel abuse at Hucheng.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Jun parlayed Emperor Wu’s favor into a post he never deserved; Jia Mi exploited Emperor Hui’s weakness and laid the steps to ruin—so Empress Jia met death at the Yunlin Hall, and Crown Prince Yu suffered torture and murder at Hucheng.

sentences.zh: 天人道盡，喪亂弘多，宗廟以之顛覆，黎庶於焉殄瘁。

translations.literal: The way of Heaven and men was exhausted; bereavement and chaos were vast; the ancestral temple thereby was overturned; the common people thereby were worn to the bone.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven and earth seemed to abandon the house of Jin; chaos spread without end, the altars fell, and the people were ground down.

sentences.zh: 《詩》云：「赫赫宗周，褒姒滅之。

translations.literal: The Classic of Poetry says: ‘Splendid was the Zhou of the ancestors—Baosi destroyed it.’
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Songs says: ‘Grand stood the house of Zhou—and Baosi brought it down.’

sentences.zh: 」其此之謂也。

translations.literal: ’—this is what is meant by that.
translations.idiomatic: That is exactly what happened here.

sentences.zh: 爰及江左，未改覆車。

translations.literal: Extending to the left bank of the Yangzi, they did not change the overturned cart.
translations.idiomatic: South of the river they repeated the same fatal mistake.

sentences.zh: 庾亮世族羽儀，王恭高門領袖，既而職兼出納，任切股肱。

translations.literal: Yu Liang was the plume and standard of great clans; Wang Gong was leader of eminent houses; thereafter their offices combined intake and outgo, and their charge was as close as thigh and arm.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Liang stood at the head of the great families; Wang Gong led the high-born elite; both held posts that controlled access to the throne and served as the emperor’s right arm.

sentences.zh: 孝伯竟以亡身，元規幾于敗國，豈不哀哉！

translations.literal: Xiaobo in the end thereby lost his life; Yuankui nearly thereby ruined the state—is it not lamentable!
translations.idiomatic: Wang Gong died for it; Yu Liang nearly destroyed the realm—is that not a tragedy?

sentences.zh: 若褚季野之畏避朝權，王叔仁之固求出鎮，用能全身遠害，有可稱焉。

translations.literal: As for Chu Yeye’s fearing and avoiding court power, and Wang Shuren’s firmly seeking to go out and hold a command, by this they were able to preserve the body and keep far from harm—there is something to praise in that.
translations.idiomatic: Chu Pou shrank from wielding power at court, and Wang Shu begged to be sent to the frontier; both kept their skins and their honor, and deserve mention.

sentences.zh: 賈充、楊駿、庾亮、王獻之、王恭等已入列傳，其餘既敘其成敗，以為《外戚篇》云。

translations.literal: Jia Chong, Yang Jun, Yu Liang, Wang Xianzhi, Wang Gong, and others have already entered the arrayed biographies; as for the rest, having narrated their success and failure, it is made into this ‘Imperial Affines’ chapter.
translations.idiomatic: Jia Chong, Yang Jun, Yu Liang, Wang Xianzhi, and Wang Gong already have their own chapters; what follows records the rest, gathered here under ‘Imperial Affines.’

sentences.zh: 羊琇，字稚舒，景獻皇后之從父弟也。

translations.literal: Yang Xiu, styled Zhishu, was a paternal cousin of Empress Jingxian.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Xiu, courtesy name Zhishu, was a cousin of Empress Jingxian on her father’s side.

sentences.zh: 父耽，官至太常。

translations.literal: His father Dan rose to Grand Master of Ceremonies.
translations.idiomatic: His father, Yang Dan, reached the post of Grand Master of Ceremonies.

sentences.zh: 兄瑾，尚書右僕射。

translations.literal: His elder brother Jin was Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
translations.idiomatic: His older brother Yang Jin served as Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.

sentences.zh: 琇少舉郡計，參鎮西鐘會軍事，從平蜀。

translations.literal: Xiu in youth was recommended on the commandery accounts, joined the staff of the West-Pacifying General Zhong Hui, and followed in the pacification of Shu.
translations.idiomatic: As a young man he was sent up on the commandery quota, served on Zhong Hui’s staff as West-Pacifying General, and took part in the conquest of Shu.

sentences.zh: 及會謀反，琇正言苦諫，還，賜爵關內侯。

translations.literal: When Hui plotted rebellion, Xiu with upright words bitterly remonstrated; on returning, he was enfeoffed as Marquis Within the Passes.
translations.idiomatic: When Zhong Hui rebelled, Yang Xiu spoke bluntly against it; afterward he was rewarded with the rank of Marquis Within the Passes.

sentences.zh: 琇涉學有智算，少與武帝通門，甚相親狎，每接筵同席，嘗謂帝曰：「若富貴見用，任領護各十年。

translations.literal: Xiu was versed in learning and had clever reckoning; in youth he shared gate ties with Emperor Wu and was very intimate; whenever they met at feasts on the same mat, he once said to the emperor: ‘If when noble and honored I am employed, let me hold each of Colonel of the Garrison and Protector of the Army for ten years.’
translations.idiomatic: Yang Xiu was learned and shrewd; he had known Emperor Wu since youth and they were close. At shared meals he once said, ‘If I rise with you, give me ten years as chief of each guard command.’

sentences.zh: 」帝戲而許之。

translations.literal: ’ The emperor in jest assented.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor laughed and agreed.

sentences.zh: 初，帝未立為太子，而聲論不及弟攸，文帝素意重攸，恆有代宗之議。

translations.literal: At first, when the emperor had not yet been established as heir apparent, his reputation did not match his younger brother You’s; Emperor Wen had long favored You and constantly had talk of replacing the heir.
translations.idiomatic: Before Sima Yan was named heir, opinion favored his younger brother Sima You; Emperor Wen had always preferred You, and courtiers often spoke of making You the successor.

sentences.zh: 琇密為武帝畫策，甚有匡救。

translations.literal: Xiu secretly for Emperor Wu drew plans and had great corrective rescue.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Xiu worked behind the scenes for Sima Yan and did much to steady his position.

sentences.zh: 又觀察文帝為政損益，揆度應所顧問之事，皆令武帝默而識之。

translations.literal: Further he observed Emperor Wen’s governance, what was harmful and beneficial, and estimated matters that should be consulted on, all ordering Emperor Wu silently to memorize them.
translations.idiomatic: He also studied how Emperor Wen ran the government and guessed what questions might come up, then had Sima Yan commit the answers to memory.

sentences.zh: 其後文帝與武帝論當世之務及人間可否，武帝答無不允，由是儲位遂定。

translations.literal: Thereafter when Emperor Wen discussed with Emperor Wu the tasks of the age and whether affairs among men were feasible or not, Emperor Wu’s answers were without exception fitting; by this the heir’s place was then fixed.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen later quizzed Sima Yan on policy and practical judgment, every reply was apt, and the succession was settled.

sentences.zh: 及帝為撫軍，命琇參軍事。

translations.literal: When the emperor became Army-soothing General, he ordered Xiu to join military affairs.
translations.idiomatic: When Sima Yan became General Who Pacifies the Army, he put Yang Xiu on his military staff.

sentences.zh: 帝即王位後，擢琇為左衛將軍，封甘露亭侯。

translations.literal: After the emperor assumed the kingship, he promoted Xiu to General of the Left Guard and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Sweet-Dew Hamlet.
translations.idiomatic: Once Sima Yan took the throne of Wei, he raised Yang Xiu to General of the Left Guard and made him Marquis of Sweet-Dew Hamlet.

sentences.zh: 帝踐阼，累遷中護軍，加散騎常侍。

translations.literal: When the emperor ascended the throne, he was repeatedly promoted to Central Protector of the Army and added as Regular Cavalier Attendant.
translations.idiomatic: After Sima Yan became emperor, Yang Xiu rose step by step to Central Protector of the Army with the additional title of Regular Cavalier Attendant.

sentences.zh: 琇在職十三年，典禁兵，豫機密，寵遇甚厚。

translations.literal: Xiu in office thirteen years commanded the forbidden troops, participated in secret matters, and favor and treatment were very thick.
translations.idiomatic: For thirteen years he commanded the palace guard, shared state secrets, and enjoyed extraordinary favor.

sentences.zh: 初，杜預拜鎮南將軍，朝士畢賀，皆連榻而坐。

translations.literal: At first, when Du Yu was appointed South-Pacifying General, court gentlemen all congratulated him and all sat with joined couches.
translations.idiomatic: When Du Yu was named South-Pacifying General, the whole court came to congratulate him, seating themselves on contiguous daybeds.

sentences.zh: 琇與裴楷後至，曰：「杜元凱乃復以連榻而坐客邪？

translations.literal: Xiu and Pei Kai arrived late and said: ‘Du Yuankai would again use joined couches to seat guests?’
translations.idiomatic: Yang Xiu and Pei Kai arrived late and said, ‘Is Du Yu really receiving guests sprawled on shared couches like this?’

sentences.zh: 」遂不坐而去。

translations.literal: ’ Then he did not sit and left.
translations.idiomatic: He refused to sit down and walked out.

sentences.zh: 琇性豪侈，費用無復齊限，而屑炭和作獸形以溫酒，洛下豪貴咸競效之。

translations.literal: Xiu by nature was grand and extravagant; expenditure no longer had even limit, and he shaved charcoal and mixed it to make beast shapes to warm wine; Luoyang’s grandees all vied to imitate it.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Xiu lived lavishly beyond measure; he shaped charcoal dust into animals to heat his wine, and the Luoyang elite rushed to copy him.

sentences.zh: 又喜游燕，以夜續晝，中外五親無男女之別，時人譏之。

translations.literal: Further he delighted in roaming feasts, using night to continue day; inner and outer, five degrees of kin had no distinction of men and women, and people of the time ridiculed him.
translations.idiomatic: He loved all-night parties that ran from dusk to dawn, with kinsmen of every degree mingling without regard to sex; contemporaries mocked him for it.

sentences.zh: 然黨慕勝己，其所推舉，便盡心無二。

translations.literal: Yet he factionally admired those better than himself; those whom he recommended, then, he served with whole heart without duplicity.
translations.idiomatic: Yet he championed men he deemed his betters and, once he backed someone, backed him wholeheartedly.

sentences.zh: 窮窘之徒，特能振恤。

translations.literal: Those in destitution and straits, he was especially able to relieve and pity.
translations.idiomatic: He was unusually generous to friends fallen on hard times.

sentences.zh: 選用多以得意者居先，不盡銓次之理。

translations.literal: In selection and employment mostly those who pleased him came first; he did not exhaust the principle of ordered ranking.
translations.idiomatic: In appointments he favored his own picks over proper seniority.

sentences.zh: 將士有冒官位者，為其致節，不惜軀命。

translations.literal: Among generals and soldiers there were those who falsely claimed official rank; for them he extended utmost loyalty and did not spare body and life.
translations.idiomatic: If soldiers had finagled rank on his recommendation, he would stake his life to protect them.

sentences.zh: 然放恣犯法，每為有司所貸。

translations.literal: Yet unrestrained he violated the law and was always forgiven by the authorities.
translations.idiomatic: He broke the law with impunity; officials usually looked the other way.

sentences.zh: 其後司隸校尉劉毅劾之，應至重刑，武帝以舊恩，直免官而已。

translations.literal: Thereafter Metropolitan Commandant Liu Yi impeached him; it should have reached heavy punishment, but Emperor Wu on account of old favor only dismissed him from office.
translations.idiomatic: When Metropolitan Commandant Liu Yi impeached him, the case called for severe penalties, but Emperor Wu settled for stripping him of his post out of old friendship.

sentences.zh: 尋以侯白衣領護軍。

translations.literal: Soon, as marquis in white garments he headed the Protector of the Army.
translations.idiomatic: Before long he was allowed to retain his marquisate while serving as Protector of the Army in civilian dress.

sentences.zh: 頃之，復職。

translations.literal: In a short while, he was restored to office.
translations.idiomatic: He was soon reinstated.

sentences.zh: 及齊王攸出鎮也，琇以切諫忤旨，左遷太僕。

translations.literal: When Prince of Qi You went out to hold a command, Xiu with cutting remonstrance offended the intent and was demoted left to Grand Coachman.
translations.idiomatic: When Sima You was sent to a provincial command, Yang Xiu’s blunt opposition angered the throne and he was demoted to Grand Coachman.

sentences.zh: 既失寵憤怨，遂發病，以疾篤求退。

translations.literal: Having lost favor, angry and resentful, he then fell ill; on account of grave illness he sought to retire.
translations.idiomatic: Spurned and bitter, he fell sick and asked to retire on grounds of ill health.

sentences.zh: 拜特進，加散騎常侍，還第，卒。

translations.literal: He was appointed Exalted Marcher, added as Regular Cavalier Attendant, returned to his mansion, and died.
translations.idiomatic: He was given the honorific Exalted Marcher and Regular Cavalier Attendant, went home, and died.

sentences.zh: 帝手詔曰：「琇與朕有先後之親，少小之恩，歷位外內，忠允茂著。

translations.literal: The emperor’s handwritten edict said: ‘Xiu with Us has closeness of empress and consort, favor from youth, has passed through posts outer and inner, loyalty and trustworthiness luxuriantly manifest.’
translations.idiomatic: The emperor wrote by his own hand: ‘Yang Xiu is kin by marriage and has known Us since boyhood; he has served inside and outside the court with conspicuous loyalty.’

sentences.zh: 不幸早薨，朕甚悼之。

translations.literal: ’ Unluckily he died early; We greatly mourn him.
translations.idiomatic: His early death grieves Us deeply.’

sentences.zh: 其追贈輔國大將軍、開府儀同三司，賜東園秘器，朝服一襲，錢三十萬，布百匹。

translations.literal: Let him be posthumously awarded General Who Aids the State, opener of office, peer with the Three Dukes; grant Eastern Park secret coffin gear, one set of court dress, three hundred thousand cash, one hundred bolts of cloth.
translations.idiomatic: Posthumously award him General Who Aids the State with full ministerial establishment, a state funeral coffin set, one court robe, three hundred thousand cash, and a hundred bolts of cloth.

sentences.zh: 」諡曰威。

translations.literal: ’ His posthumous name was Wei (‘Formidable’).
translations.idiomatic: He was given the posthumous name Wei, ‘the Formidable.’

sentences.zh: 王恂，字良夫，文明皇后之弟也。

translations.literal: Wang Xun, styled Liangfu, was the younger brother of Empress Wenming.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Xun, courtesy name Liangfu, was a younger brother of Empress Wenming.

sentences.zh: 父肅，魏蘭陵侯。

translations.literal: His father Su was Marquis of Lanling under Wei.
translations.idiomatic: His father Wang Su held the Wei title of Marquis of Lanling.

sentences.zh: 恂文義通博，在朝忠正，累遷河南尹，建立二學，崇明《五經》。

translations.literal: Xun in letters and meaning was comprehensive and broad; in court loyal and upright; he was repeatedly promoted to Intendant of Henan, established two schools, and exalted the Five Classics.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Xun was learned and upright at court, rose to Intendant of Henan, founded two academies, and promoted study of the Five Classics.

sentences.zh: 鬲令袁毅嘗饋以駿馬，恂不受。

translations.literal: Magistrate of Ge Yuan Yi once presented fine horses; Xun did not accept.
translations.idiomatic: Yuan Yi, magistrate of Ge, once offered him fine horses; Wang Xun refused them.

sentences.zh: 及毅敗，受貨者皆被廢黜焉。

translations.literal: When Yi was ruined, those who had received goods were all dismissed and degraded.
translations.idiomatic: When Yuan Yi fell, everyone who had taken his gifts was cashiered.

sentences.zh: 魏氏給公卿已下租牛客戶數各有差，自後小人憚役，多樂為之，貴勢之門動有百數。

translations.literal: The Wei house granted to dukes and ministers downward rental-ox client households in numbers each with differences; thereafter petty men feared corvée and mostly delighted to become them; doors of noble power often had hundreds.
translations.idiomatic: Wei had allotted tenant farmers and draft oxen to officials down the ladder; commoners dodged labor service by attaching themselves to great houses, and a single magnate might shelter hundreds of such clients.

sentences.zh: 又太原諸部亦以匈奴胡人為田客，多者數千。

translations.literal: Further in Taiyuan’s various divisions they also used Xiongnu Hu people as field clients; in many cases several thousand.
translations.idiomatic: In Taiyuan, magnates also took Xiongnu herders as tenant farmers—some in the thousands.

sentences.zh: 武帝踐位，詔禁募客，恂明峻其防，所部莫敢犯者。

translations.literal: When Emperor Wu ascended the throne, he ordered a ban on recruiting clients; Xun made bright and severe its defenses; in what was under his charge none dared violate it.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wu forbade the practice; Wang Xun enforced the rule so strictly in his jurisdiction that no one dared break it.

sentences.zh: 咸寧四年卒，贈車騎將軍。

translations.literal: In the fourth year of Xianning he died; he was posthumously awarded General of Chariots and Cavalry.
translations.idiomatic: He died in 278 and was posthumously named General of Chariots and Cavalry.

sentences.zh: 恂弟虔、愷。

translations.literal: Xun’s younger brothers were Qian and Kai.
translations.idiomatic: His brothers were Wang Qian and Wang Kai.

sentences.zh: 虔字恭祖。

translations.literal: Qian styled Gongzu.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Qian’s courtesy name was Gongzu.

sentences.zh: 以功幹見稱，累遷衛尉，封安壽亭侯，拜平東將軍、假節、監青州諸軍事。

translations.literal: He was praised for merit and capacity; he was repeatedly promoted to Commandant of the Guards, enfeoffed as Marquis of Anshou Hamlet, appointed East-Pacifying General, given credentials, and overseer of Qingzhou military affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Known for ability and achievement, he rose to Commandant of the Guards, was made Marquis of Anshou Hamlet, and became East-Pacifying General with credentials and command over Qingzhou forces.

sentences.zh: 徵為光祿勳，轉尚書，卒。

translations.literal: He was summoned as Supervisor of the Household, transferred to Director in the Department of State Affairs, and died.
translations.idiomatic: He was recalled as Supervisor of the Household, then Director in the Department of State Affairs, and died in office.

sentences.zh: 子士文嗣，歷右衛將軍、南中郎將，鎮許昌，為劉聰所害。

translations.literal: His son Shiwen succeeded; he passed through General of the Right Guard, General of the Southern Gentlemen of the Household, garrisoned Xuchang, and was killed by Liu Cong.
translations.idiomatic: His heir Wang Shiwen served as General of the Right Guard and Southern Gentlemen leader, held Xuchang, and was killed by Liu Cong.

sentences.zh: 愷字君夫。

translations.literal: Kai styled Junfu.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Kai’s courtesy name was Junfu.

sentences.zh: 少有才力，歷位清顯，雖無細行，有在公之稱。

translations.literal: In youth he had talent and strength; he passed through posts pure and eminent; though he had no fine conduct in small things, he had a reputation for public-mindedness.
translations.idiomatic: Capable from youth, he rose to high office; though his private morals were loose, he was thought diligent in public duty.

sentences.zh: 以討楊駿勳，封山都縣公，邑千八百戶。

translations.literal: On account of merit in punishing Yang Jun, he was enfeoffed as Duke of Shandu County, fief of one thousand eight hundred households.
translations.idiomatic: For his part in bringing down Yang Jun he was made Duke of Shandu with eighteen hundred households.

sentences.zh: 遷龍驤將軍，領驍騎將軍，加散騎常侍，尋坐事免官。

translations.literal: He was promoted to Dragon-Prancing General, concurrent Valiant Cavalry General, added as Regular Cavalier Attendant; soon he sat on a matter and was dismissed from office.
translations.idiomatic: He advanced to Dragon-Prancing General and Valiant Cavalry commander with the additional title of Regular Cavalier Attendant, then lost his posts after an incident.

sentences.zh: 起為射聲校尉，久之，轉後將軍。

translations.literal: He was raised as Colonel of the Sound-of-the-Bowstring Archers; after a long time, he was transferred to Rear General.
translations.idiomatic: He was brought back as Colonel of the Sound-of-the-Bowstring Archers and later became Rear General.

sentences.zh: 愷既世族國戚，性復豪侈，用赤石脂泥壁。

translations.literal: Kai was both a great-clan man and state kin; his nature was again grand and extravagant; he used red halloysite to mud walls.
translations.idiomatic: As both a great-clan magnate and imperial in-law, Wang Kai lived in ostentatious luxury, plastering his walls with costly red bole.

sentences.zh: 石崇與愷將為鴆毒之事，司隸校尉傅祗劾之，有司皆論正重罪，詔特原之。

translations.literal: Shi Chong and Kai were about to do a matter of zhen poison; Metropolitan Commandant Fu Di impeached them; the authorities all judged proper heavy crimes; an edict specially pardoned them.
translations.idiomatic: When he and Shi Chong were implicated in a plot to poison each other, Metropolitan Commandant Fu Di impeached them; the courts recommended harsh sentences, but an imperial edict let them off.

sentences.zh: 由是眾人僉畏愷，故敢肆其意，所欲之事無所顧憚焉。

translations.literal: By this all men equally feared Kai; therefore he dared unleash his intent; in matters he desired there was nothing he looked to or feared.
translations.idiomatic: Thereafter everyone feared him, and he indulged every whim without scruple.

sentences.zh: 及卒，諡曰醜。

translations.literal: When he died, his posthumous name was Chou (‘Ugly’).
translations.idiomatic: At his death he received the harsh posthumous name Chou, ‘the Repulsive.’

sentences.zh: 楊文宗

translations.literal: Yang Wenzong
translations.idiomatic: Yang Wenzong

sentences.zh: 楊文宗，武元皇后父也。

translations.literal: Yang Wenzong was the father of Empress Wuyuan.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Wenzong was the father of Empress Wuyuan.

sentences.zh: 其先事漢，四世為三公。

translations.literal: His ancestors served Han; for four generations they were the Three Dukes.
translations.idiomatic: His family had served Han, with four generations holding one of the Three Dukes’ posts.

sentences.zh: 文宗為魏通事郎，襲封蓩亭侯。

translations.literal: Wenzong was Wei’s Master of Communications and inherited enfeoffment as Marquis of Mao Hamlet.
translations.idiomatic: He served Wei as Master of Communications and inherited the marquisate of Mao Hamlet.

sentences.zh: 早卒，以后父，追贈車騎將軍，諡曰穆。

translations.literal: He died early; on account of being the empress’s father, he was posthumously awarded General of Chariots and Cavalry; his posthumous name was Mu (‘Solemn’).
translations.idiomatic: He died young; as the empress’s father he was posthumously named General of Chariots and Cavalry with the posthumous title Mu, ‘the Solemn.’

sentences.zh: 羊玄之

translations.literal: Yang Xuanzhi
translations.idiomatic: Yang Xuanzhi

sentences.zh: 羊玄之，惠皇后父，尚書右僕射瑾之子也。

translations.literal: Yang Xuanzhi was the father of Empress Hui and the son of Right Vice Director Jin.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Xuanzhi, father of Empress Hui, was the son of Yang Jin, Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.

sentences.zh: 玄之初為尚書郎，以后父，拜光祿大夫、特進、散騎常侍，更封興晉侯。

translations.literal: Xuanzhi at first was a Gentleman of the Department of State Affairs; on account of being the empress’s father, he was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Carriage, Exalted Marcher, Regular Cavalier Attendant, and re-enfeoffed as Marquis Who Rouses Jin.
translations.idiomatic: He began as a junior secretary in the Department of State Affairs; as the empress’s father he rose to Grand Master of Splendid Carriage, Exalted Marcher, and Regular Cavalier Attendant, and was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Rising Jin.

sentences.zh: 遷尚書右僕射，加侍中，進爵為公。

translations.literal: He was promoted to Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, added as Palace Attendant, and advanced in nobility to duke.
translations.idiomatic: He became Right Vice Director, was given the additional post of Palace Attendant, and was raised to ducal rank.

sentences.zh: 成都王穎之攻長沙王乂也，以討玄之為名，遂憂懼而卒。

translations.literal: When Prince of Chengdu Ying attacked Prince of Changsha Yi, taking punishing Xuanzhi as the name, then in worry and fear he died.
translations.idiomatic: When Sima Ying marched against Sima Yi under the pretext of punishing Yang Xuanzhi, Xuanzhi died of fear and anxiety.

sentences.zh: 追贈車騎將軍、開府儀同三司。

translations.literal: He was posthumously awarded General of Chariots and Cavalry, opener of office, peer with the Three Dukes.
translations.idiomatic: He was posthumously honored as General of Chariots and Cavalry with full Three Dukes’ establishment.

sentences.zh: 虞豫，元敬皇后父也。

translations.literal: Yu Yu was the father of Empress Yuanjing.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Yu was the father of Empress Yuanjing.

sentences.zh: 少有美稱，州郡禮辟，並不就。

translations.literal: In youth he had a fine reputation; commanderies and prefectures with ritual summoned him, and he did not go to any.
translations.idiomatic: Praised from youth, he turned down every official summons from local authorities.

sentences.zh: 拜南陽王文學。

translations.literal: He was appointed literary instructor to the Prince of Nanyang.
translations.idiomatic: He accepted appointment as tutor in letters to the Prince of Nanyang.

sentences.zh: 早卒。

translations.literal: He died early.
translations.idiomatic: He died young.

sentences.zh: 明帝即位，追贈散騎常侍、驃騎大將軍、開府儀同三司、平山縣侯。

translations.literal: When Emperor Ming ascended the throne, he was posthumously awarded Regular Cavalier Attendant, Grand General Who Gallops as if Flying, opener of office peer with the Three Dukes, and Marquis of Pingshan County.
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor Ming took the throne, Yu Yu was posthumously named Regular Cavalier Attendant, Grand General Who Gallops as if Flying, with ministerial establishment, and Marquis of Pingshan.

sentences.zh: 子胤嗣。

translations.literal: His son Yin succeeded.
translations.idiomatic: His son Yu Yin inherited the title.

sentences.zh: 庾琛，字子美，明穆皇后父也。

translations.literal: Yu Chen, styled Zimei, was the father of Empress Mingmu.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Chen, courtesy name Zimei, was the father of Empress Mingmu.

sentences.zh: 兄袞，在《孝友傳》。

translations.literal: His elder brother Gun is in the ‘Filial and Friendly’ biographies.
translations.idiomatic: His brother Yu Gun has a biography in the chapter on filial sons and devoted brothers.

sentences.zh: 琛永嘉初為建威將軍，過江，為會稽太守，徵為丞相軍諮祭酒。

translations.literal: Chen in the beginning of Yongjia was General Who Establishes Might; he crossed the Yangzi and became Administrator of Kuaiji; he was summoned as libationer for army consultation under the Chancellor.
translations.idiomatic: Early in the Yongjia era he served as General Who Establishes Might, crossed south of the Yangzi, became Administrator of Kuaiji, and was then recalled as Army Adviser and Libationer on the chancellor’s staff.

sentences.zh: 卒官，以后父追贈左將軍，妻毌丘氏追封鄉君，子亮陳先志不受。

translations.literal: He died in office; on account of being the empress’s father he was posthumously awarded General of the Left; his wife Lady Guanqiu was posthumously enfeoffed as Village Mistress; his son Liang stated his late father’s intent and did not accept.
translations.idiomatic: He died in office. The court would have honored him posthumously as General of the Left and his wife Lady Guanqiu as a village matron, but Yu Liang cited his father’s wishes and declined the honors.

sentences.zh: 咸和中，成帝又下詔追贈琛驃騎將軍、儀同三司，亮又辭焉。

translations.literal: In the Xianhe era, Emperor Cheng again issued an edict posthumously awarding Chen Grand General Who Gallops as if Flying, peer in ceremony with the Three Dukes; Liang again declined.
translations.idiomatic: During Xianhe, Emperor Cheng again ordered posthumous honors for Yu Chen as Grand General Who Gallops as if Flying with Three Dukes’ ceremony; Yu Liang refused once more.

sentences.zh: 亮在列傳。

translations.literal: Liang is in the arrayed biographies.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Liang has his own biography elsewhere.

sentences.zh: 杜乂，字弘理，成恭皇后父，鎮南將軍預孫，尚書左丞錫之子也。

translations.literal: Du Yi, styled Hongli, was the father of Empress Chenggong, grandson of South-Pacifying General Yu, and son of Left Assistant Director Xi.
translations.idiomatic: Du Yi, courtesy name Hongli, father of Empress Chenggong, was a grandson of Du Yu, South-Pacifying General, and son of Du Xi, Left Assistant Director in the Department of State Affairs.

sentences.zh: 性純和，美姿容，有盛名于江左。

translations.literal: By nature pure and mild, handsome in bearing, he had a great reputation south of the Yangzi.
translations.idiomatic: Gentle in temper and strikingly handsome, he was famous throughout the south.

sentences.zh: 王羲之見而目之曰：「膚若凝脂，眼如點漆，此神仙人也。

translations.literal: Wang Xizhi saw him and marked him, saying: ‘Skin like congealed fat, eyes like dabs of lacquer—this is an immortal among men.’
translations.idiomatic: Wang Xizhi said of him, ‘His skin is like curdled cream, his eyes like drops of ink—he might be an immortal walking among us.’

sentences.zh: 」桓彝亦曰：「衛玠神清，杜乂形清。

translations.literal: ’ Huan Yi also said: ‘Wei Jie is clear in spirit; Du Yi is clear in form.’
translations.idiomatic: Huan Yi added, ‘Wei Jie shines in spirit; Du Yi shines in the flesh.’

sentences.zh: 」襲封當陽侯，辟公府掾，為丹陽丞。

translations.literal: ’ He inherited enfeoffment as Marquis of Dangyang, was summoned as a clerk in the duke’s office, and became Assistant to the Administrator of Danyang.
translations.idiomatic: He inherited the marquisate of Danyang, served on a commandery staff, and was appointed assistant magistrate of Danyang.

sentences.zh: 早卒，無男，生后而乂終，妻裴氏嫠居養后，以禮自防，甚有德音。

translations.literal: He died early, without sons; the empress was born and then Yi ended; his wife Lady Pei as widow dwelt rearing the empress, by ritual guarding herself, and had very virtuous repute.
translations.idiomatic: He died young and sonless soon after his daughter was born. Lady Pei raised the girl alone, kept strict propriety as a widow, and was widely praised.

sentences.zh: 咸康初，追贈金紫光祿大夫，諡曰穆。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Xiankang, he was posthumously awarded Grand Master of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon; his posthumous name was Mu (‘Solemn’).
translations.idiomatic: Early in Xiankang he was posthumously named Grand Master of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon with the posthumous title Mu.

sentences.zh: 封裴氏為高安鄉君，邑五百戶。

translations.literal: Lady Pei was enfeoffed as Village Mistress of Gao’an, fief of five hundred households.
translations.idiomatic: Lady Pei was made Village Mistress of Gao’an with a fief of five hundred households.

sentences.zh: 至孝武帝時，崇進為廣德縣君。

translations.literal: By the time of Emperor Xiaowu, she was advanced in honor to County Mistress of Guangde.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Xiaowu her title was raised to County Mistress of Guangde.

sentences.zh: 裴氏壽考，百姓號曰杜姥。

translations.literal: Lady Pei lived to great age; the common people called her Granny Du.
translations.idiomatic: Lady Pei lived to a ripe old age, and folk called her ‘Granny Du.’

sentences.zh: 初，司徒蔡謨甚器重乂，嘗言於朝曰：「恨諸君不見杜乂也。

translations.literal: At first, Minister of Education Cai Mo greatly esteemed Yi and once said at court: ‘I regret that you gentlemen have not seen Du Yi.’
translations.idiomatic: Minister Cai Mo thought the world of Du Yi and once told the court, ‘It is your loss never to have laid eyes on Du Yi.’

sentences.zh: 」其為名流所重如此。

translations.literal: ’ Thus was he esteemed by the famous and eminent.
translations.idiomatic: Such was the regard the leading men of the age had for him.

sentences.zh: 褚裒，字季野，康獻皇后父也。

translations.literal: Chu Pou, styled Yeye, was the father of Empress Kangxian.
translations.idiomatic: Chu Pou, courtesy name Yeye, was the father of Empress Kangxian.

sentences.zh: 祖䂮，有局量，以幹用稱。

translations.literal: His grandfather Lü had breadth of mind and was praised for capacity and usefulness.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather Chu Lü was broad-minded and valued for practical ability.

sentences.zh: 嘗為縣吏，事有不合，令欲鞭之，䂮曰：「物各有所施，榱椽之材不合以為籓落也，願明府垂察。

translations.literal: He once was a county clerk; when a matter did not accord, the magistrate wished to flog him; Lü said: ‘Things each have their use; rafter timber is not fit to be a hedge fence; I beg the enlightened prefect to look into it.’
translations.idiomatic: As a county clerk he once crossed his magistrate, who meant to whip him. Chu Lü said, ‘Every material has its proper use—one does not make a fence from roof beams. I ask you to reconsider.’

sentences.zh: 」乃舍之。

translations.literal: ’ Then he released him.
translations.idiomatic: The magistrate let him go.

sentences.zh: 家貧，辭吏。

translations.literal: The family was poor; he resigned the clerkship.
translations.idiomatic: Poor at home, he gave up the post.

sentences.zh: 年垂五十，鎮南將軍羊祜與䂮有舊，言于武帝，始被升用，官至安東將軍。

translations.literal: His years nearing fifty, South-Pacifying General Yang Hu, who had old ties with Lü, spoke to Emperor Wu; then he first was promoted and employed, his office reaching East-securing General.
translations.idiomatic: Near fifty, he was finally recommended to Emperor Wu by his old acquaintance Yang Hu, South-Pacifying General, and rose to East-securing General.

sentences.zh: 父洽，武昌太守。

translations.literal: His father Qia was Administrator of Wuchang.
translations.idiomatic: His father Chu Qia had been Administrator of Wuchang.

sentences.zh: 裒少有簡貴之風，與京兆杜乂俱有盛名，冠于中興。

translations.literal: Pou in youth had a manner aloof and noble; together with Du Yi of Jingzhao he had a great reputation, foremost in the Restoration.
translations.idiomatic: In youth Chu Pou shared with Du Yi of Jingzhao the highest reputation of the restored court.

sentences.zh: 譙國桓彝見而目之曰：「季野有皮裏春秋。

translations.literal: Huan Yi of Qiao saw him and marked him, saying: ‘Yeye has a Spring and Autumn inside the skin.’
translations.idiomatic: Huan Yi said of him, ‘Chu Pou keeps a private verdict under a calm face.’

sentences.zh: 」言其外無臧否，而內有所褒貶也。

translations.literal: ’—meaning outwardly he had no praise or blame, but inwardly he had commendation and censure.
translations.idiomatic: That is, he seemed neutral in public while judging people inwardly.

sentences.zh: 謝安亦雅重之，恆云：「裒雖不言，而四時之氣亦備矣。

translations.literal: Xie An also greatly esteemed him, always saying: ‘Though Pou does not speak, the qi of the four seasons is also complete in him.’
translations.idiomatic: Xie An likewise admired him, remarking, ‘Chu Pou need not speak; he already holds all four seasons in his bearing.’

sentences.zh: 」初辟西陽王掾、吳王文學。

translations.literal: ’ At first he was summoned as clerk to the Prince of Xiyang and literary instructor to the Prince of Wu.
translations.idiomatic: He began as a staff officer to the Prince of Xiyang and tutor in letters to the Prince of Wu.

sentences.zh: 蘇峻之構逆也，車騎將軍郗鑒以裒為參軍。

translations.literal: When Su Jun plotted rebellion, General of Chariots and Cavalry Xi Jian made Pou his army adviser.
translations.idiomatic: During Su Jun’s revolt, Xi Jian, General of Chariots and Cavalry, appointed him to his staff.

sentences.zh: 峻平，以功封都鄉亭侯，稍遷司徒從事中郎，除給事黃門侍郎。

translations.literal: When Jun was pacified, on account of merit he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Duxiang Hamlet, gradually promoted to Consultant in the Bureau of the Minister of Education, and appointed Palace Attendant and Gentleman at the Yellow Gate.
translations.idiomatic: After the victory he was made Marquis of Duxiang Hamlet, then rose to consultant on the minister’s staff and Palace Attendant at the Yellow Gate.

sentences.zh: 康帝為琅邪王時，將納妃，妙選素望，詔娉裒女為妃，於是出為豫章太守。

translations.literal: When Emperor Kang was Prince of Langye, about to take a consort, with subtle selection of plain repute, an edict betrothed Pou’s daughter as consort; thereupon he went out as Administrator of Yuzhang.
translations.idiomatic: While still Prince of Langye, Emperor Kang chose Chu Pou’s daughter for his bride; to avoid impropriety Chu Pou took a post away from the capital as Administrator of Yuzhang.

sentences.zh: 及康帝即位，徵拜侍中，遷尚書。

translations.literal: When Emperor Kang ascended the throne, he was summoned and appointed Palace Attendant, promoted to Director in the Department of State Affairs.
translations.idiomatic: After Emperor Kang’s accession he was recalled as Palace Attendant and then Director in the Department of State Affairs.

sentences.zh: 以后父，苦求外出，除建威將軍、江州刺史，鎮半洲。

translations.literal: On account of being the empress’s father, he bitterly sought to go out; he was appointed General Who Establishes Might, Inspector of Jiangzhou, and garrisoned Banzhou.
translations.idiomatic: Unwilling to loom over the court as the empress’s father, he begged for a provincial post and became General Who Establishes Might and Inspector of Jiangzhou, stationed at Banzhou.

sentences.zh: 在官清約，雖居方伯，恆使私童樵採。

translations.literal: In office clear and abstemious, though he dwelt as a regional lord, he always made private lads gather firewood.
translations.idiomatic: He lived simply even as a regional inspector, sending his own servants to cut firewood rather than burden the people.

sentences.zh: 頃之，徵為衛將軍，領中書令。

translations.literal: In a short while, he was summoned as General of the Guards, concurrent Director of the Palace Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: Soon he was recalled as General of the Guards and overseer of the Palace Secretariat.

sentences.zh: 裒以中書銓管詔命，不宜以姻戚居之，固讓，詔以為左將卦、兗州刺史、都督兗州徐州之琅邪諸軍事、假節，鎮金城，又領琅邪內史。

translations.literal: Pou held that the Palace Secretariat manages and controls edicts and commands, and it was not fitting that affinal kin hold it; he firmly declined; an edict made him General of the Left, Inspector of Yanzhou, military overseer of Yanzhou and Xuzhou and Langye affairs, with credentials, garrisoned Jincheng, and also concurrent interior secretary of Langye.
translations.idiomatic: Chu Pou argued that the secretariat must not be run by an imperial in-law and refused the post. The court instead named him General of the Left, Inspector of Yanzhou, and commander of Yan, Xu, and Langye forces with credentials, stationed at Jincheng, while he also served as interior secretary of Langye.

sentences.zh: 初，裒總角詣庾亮，亮使郭璞筮之。

translations.literal: At first, when Pou in his hair-tied youth went to visit Yu Liang, Liang had Guo Pu cast milfoil for him.
translations.idiomatic: Once, while still a boy visiting Yu Liang, Chu Pou had his fate divined by Guo Pu at Liang’s request.

sentences.zh: 卦成，璞駭然，亮曰：「有不祥乎？

translations.literal: When the hexagram was complete, Pu was alarmed; Liang said: ‘Is there ill augury?’
translations.idiomatic: When the hexagram came out, Guo Pu blanched. Yu Liang asked, ‘Is the omen bad?’

sentences.zh: 」璞曰：「此非人臣卦，不知此年少何以乃表斯祥？

translations.literal: ’ Pu said: ‘This is not a subject’s hexagram; I do not know how this youth could thus display such auspice?’
translations.idiomatic: Guo Pu replied, ‘This is no pattern for a mere minister. I cannot say how this boy draws such a sign.’

sentences.zh: 二十年外，吾言方驗。

translations.literal: Beyond twenty years, my words will then be verified.’
translations.idiomatic: Wait twenty years, and you will see that I was right.

sentences.zh: 」及此二十九年而康獻皇太后臨朝，有司以裒皇太后父，議加不臣之禮，拜侍中、衛將軍、錄尚書事，持節、都督、刺史如故。

translations.literal: ’ When it came to this, in the twenty-ninth year Empress Dowager Kangxian faced the court; the authorities, because Pou was the empress dowager’s father, debated adding the rite of not being subject; he was appointed Palace Attendant, General of the Guards, Recorder of Department of State Affairs matters, holding credentials, overseer, and inspector as before.
translations.idiomatic: Twenty-nine years later, when Empress Dowager Kangxian ruled as regent, officials proposed extraordinary honors for her father: Palace Attendant, General of the Guards, and recorder of the Department of State Affairs, while he kept his credentials, command, and inspectorship.

sentences.zh: 裒以近戚，懼獲譏嫌，上疏固請居籓，曰：「臣以虛鄙，才不周用，過蒙國恩，累忝非據。

translations.literal: Pou, as close kin, feared incurring ridicule and suspicion; he submitted a memorial firmly begging to dwell in a fief, saying: ‘Your subject, with hollow baseness, talent not sufficient for use, has unduly received the state’s grace and repeatedly been shamed by unfit posts.’
translations.idiomatic: Fearing gossip as the empress dowager’s kin, Chu Pou begged to stay in the provinces: ‘I am untalented and unworthy, yet the state has heaped honors on me beyond my deserts.’

sentences.zh: 無勞受寵，負愧實深，豈可復加殊特之命，顯號重疊！

translations.literal: Without labor receiving favor, the burden of shame is truly deep—how can there again be added extraordinary special commands, illustrious titles piled atop one another!’
translations.idiomatic: I am ashamed enough without fresh favor—how can I accept still more exalted titles heaped one on another?’

sentences.zh: 臣有何勳可以克堪？

translations.literal: What merit does your subject have by which he could endure it?’
translations.idiomatic: What deed of mine could justify such reward?’

sentences.zh: 何顏可以冒進？

translations.literal: With what face could he rashly advance?’
translations.idiomatic: What face have I to accept promotion?’

sentences.zh: 委身聖世，豈復遺力，實懼顛墜，所誤者大。

translations.literal: Committing body to the sage age, how again leave strength unused—truly I fear overturning and falling; what would be missed is great.’
translations.idiomatic: I owe the throne my utmost, yet I fear a misstep would do grave harm.’

sentences.zh: 今王略未振，萬機至殷，陛下宜委誠宰輔，一遵先帝任賢之道，虛己受成，坦平心於天下，無宜內示私親之舉，朝野失望，所損豈少！

translations.literal: Now the kingly plan is not yet roused, myriad tasks are extremely numerous; Your Majesty ought to entrust sincerity to the chief ministers, wholly follow the late emperor’s way of employing the worthy, empty self and receive completion, level heart openly to the world—it is not fitting inwardly to show moves of private kinship; court and wild would lose hope—how could the harm be slight!’
translations.idiomatic: The realm is still unsettled and business presses; Your Majesty should lean on your chief ministers and follow the late emperors’ habit of trusting able men. Open your heart to the empire instead of elevating kin—the court and the countryside would lose heart, and the cost would be immense.’

sentences.zh: 」於是改授都督徐兗青揚州之晉陵吳國諸軍事、衛將軍、徐兗二州刺史、假節、鎮京口。

translations.literal: ’ Thereupon he was reassigned military overseer of Xuzhou, Yanzhou, Qingzhou, and Yangzhou’s Jinling and Wu princedom affairs, General of the Guards, dual Inspector of Xuzhou and Yanzhou, with credentials, garrisoned Jingkou.
translations.idiomatic: The court relented and named him commander of forces in Xu, Yan, Qing, and Yang (including Jinling and Wu), General of the Guards, dual inspector of Xu and Yan, with credentials, stationed at Jingkou.

sentences.zh: 永和初，復徵裒，將以為揚州、錄尚書事。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Yonghe, Pou was again summoned, about to be made Yangzhou and recorder of Department of State Affairs matters.
translations.idiomatic: Early in Yonghe he was recalled to take Yangzhou and the recordership of the Department of State Affairs.

sentences.zh: 吏部尚書劉遐說裒曰：「會稽王令德，國之周公也，足下宜以大政付之。

translations.literal: Director of the Ministry of Personnel Liu Xia said to Pou: ‘The Prince of Kuaiji’s excellent virtue—he is the house’s Duke of Zhou; you ought to entrust great government to him.’
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xia told him, ‘The Prince of Kuaiji is the Duke of Zhou of our day—you should leave supreme power in his hands.’

sentences.zh: 」裒長史王胡之亦勸焉，於是固辭歸籓，朝野咸嘆服之。

translations.literal: ’ Pou’s chief clerk Wang Huzhi also urged it; thereupon he firmly declined and returned to his fief; court and wild all sighed and admired him.
translations.idiomatic: His chief clerk Wang Huzhi said the same, so Chu Pou stood aside and returned to his command; court and country admired his restraint.

sentences.zh: 進號征北大將軍、開府儀同三司，固辭開府。

translations.literal: He was advanced in title to North-Conquering Grand General, opener of office peer with the Three Dukes; he firmly declined the opener of office.
translations.idiomatic: He was promoted to North-Conquering Grand General with Three Dukes’ establishment but refused the separate headquarters.

sentences.zh: 裒又以政道在於得才，宜委賢任能，升敬舊齒，乃薦前光祿大夫顧和、侍中殷浩。

translations.literal: Pou further held that the way of government lies in obtaining talent, that it was fitting to entrust the worthy and employ the able, and advance and revere old seniority; thereupon he recommended former Grand Master of Splendid Carriage Gu He and Palace Attendant Yin Hao.
translations.idiomatic: Believing good government depends on the right men, he urged the throne to elevate veterans and named Gu He and Yin Hao for high office.

sentences.zh: 疏奏，即以和為尚書令，浩為揚州刺史。

translations.literal: When the memorial was presented, He was immediately made Director of the Department of State Affairs and Hao Inspector of Yangzhou.
translations.idiomatic: The court accepted at once: Gu He became director of the Department of State Affairs, Yin Hao inspector of Yangzhou.

sentences.zh: 及石季龍死，裒上表請伐之，即日戒嚴，直指泗口。

translations.literal: When Shi Jilong died, Pou submitted a memorial requesting to punish him; that very day martial law was declared, aiming straight at Sikou.
translations.idiomatic: After Shi Hu’s death Chu Pou memorialized for an expedition; the army mobilized the same day toward Sikou.

sentences.zh: 朝議以裒事任貴重，不宜深入，可先遣偏師。

translations.literal: Court deliberation held that Pou’s charge was noble and weighty, not fitting to go deep; a detached column could first be sent.
translations.idiomatic: The court thought his rank too exalted for a risky advance and favored sending a smaller force first.

sentences.zh: 裒重陳前所遣前鋒督護王頤之等徑造彭城，示以威信，後遣督護麋嶷進軍下邳，賊即奔潰，嶷率所領據其城池，今宜速發，以成聲勢，於是除征討大都督青、揚、徐、兗、豫五州諸軍事。

translations.literal: Pou again set forth that previously dispatched vanguard superintending protector Wang Yizhi and others went straight to Pengcheng, displaying authority and trust; afterward superintending protector Mi Yi advanced the army to Xiapi, and the bandits at once fled in collapse; Yi led what he commanded and seized their city walls—now it is fitting to issue speedily to complete sound and momentum; thereupon he was appointed grand overseer of suppression and punishment for Qing, Yang, Xu, Yan, and Yu five provinces’ military affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Chu Pou replied that Wang Yizhi’s vanguard had already reached Pengcheng and Mi Yi had taken Xiapi, routing the enemy; a swift follow-up would consolidate the gain. He was therefore named grand commander of the five provinces’ expeditionary forces.

sentences.zh: 裒率眾三萬徑進彭城，河朔士庶歸降者日以千計，裒撫納之，甚得其歡心。

translations.literal: Pou led a host of thirty thousand straight to Pengcheng; north-of-the-He gentry and commoners who submitted came to more than a thousand a day; Pou comforted and accepted them and greatly won their joyful hearts.
translations.idiomatic: He marched thirty thousand men to Pengcheng; north of the Yellow River more than a thousand people a day came over to him, and he welcomed them so warmly that they were devoted to him.

sentences.zh: 先遣督護徐龕伐沛，獲偽相支重，郡中二千餘人歸降。

translations.literal: First he dispatched superintending protector Xu Kan to attack Pei, capturing the false chancellor Zhi Zhong; more than two thousand in the commandery submitted.
translations.idiomatic: He sent Xu Kan against Pei, captured the rival regime’s minister Zhi Zhong, and won over two thousand local people.

sentences.zh: 魯郡山有五百餘家，亦建義請援，裒遣龕領銳卒三千迎之。

translations.literal: In Lu commandery’s hills were more than five hundred households; they also raised righteousness and begged aid; Pou sent Kan leading three thousand picked soldiers to meet them.
translations.idiomatic: Five hundred hill households in Lu rose in support and begged help; Chu Pou sent Xu Kan with three thousand picked troops to link up with them.

sentences.zh: 龕違裒節度，軍次代陂，為石遵將李菟所敗，死傷太半，龕執節不撓，為賊所害。

translations.literal: Kan disobeyed Pou’s command and control; the army halted at Daipi, was defeated by Shi Zun’s general Li Tu, and dead and wounded were more than half; Kan grasped his credentials unyielding and was killed by the bandits.
translations.idiomatic: Xu Kan ignored orders, camped at Daipi, and was crushed by Li Tu, Shi Zun’s general; over half his men fell, and Kan died holding his baton of command.

sentences.zh: 裒以《春秋》責帥，授任失所，威略虧損，上疏自貶，以征北將軍行事，求留鎮廣陵。

translations.literal: Pou, by the Spring and Autumn blaming the commander, assignment losing its place, might and strategy being impaired, submitted a memorial demoting himself, acting as North-Conquering General, begging to remain and garrison Guangling.
translations.idiomatic: Invoking the principle that the commander bears blame, he memorialized to strip himself of rank, serve provisionally as North-Conquering General, and stay at Guangling.

sentences.zh: 詔以偏帥之責，不應引咎，逋寇未殄，方鎮任重，不宜貶降，使還鎮京口，解征討都督。

translations.literal: An edict held that a detached commander’s blame ought not draw reproach; the fleeing bandit was not yet exterminated; a regional post’s burden was weighty—it was not fitting to demote; he was made to return and garrison Jingkou and was relieved of grand overseer of suppression and punishment.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor replied that a subordinate’s failure should not stain him, that the enemy remained, and that his post was too important to downgrade; he was sent back to Jingkou and relieved only of the expedition command.

sentences.zh: 時石季龍新死，其國大亂，遺戶二十萬口渡河，將歸順，乞師救援。

translations.literal: At the time Shi Jilong had newly died; his state was greatly in chaos; leftover households two hundred thousand mouths crossed the river, about to submit in allegiance, begging troops for rescue.
translations.idiomatic: Shi Hu had just died and Zhao was in chaos; two hundred thousand people crossed the Yellow River seeking Jin protection and begging for an army.

sentences.zh: 會裒已旋，威勢不接，莫能自拔，皆為慕容皝及苻健之眾所掠，死亡咸盡。

translations.literal: It happened that Pou had already turned back; might and momentum did not connect; they could not save themselves; all were plundered by Murong Huang’s and Fu Jian’s hosts; death finished them all.
translations.idiomatic: But Chu Pou had already withdrawn; Jin could not reach them, and Murong Huang and Fu Jian’s troops slaughtered or enslaved them all.

sentences.zh: 裒以遠圖不就，憂慨發病。

translations.literal: Pou, because distant plans were not achieved, in worried indignation fell ill.
translations.idiomatic: The collapse of his long-range plans left him heartsick and ill.

sentences.zh: 及至京口，聞哭聲甚眾，裒問：「何哭之多？

translations.literal: When he reached Jingkou, he heard wailing voices very many; Pou asked: ‘Why so much crying?’
translations.idiomatic: At Jingkou he heard much weeping and asked why.

sentences.zh: 」左右曰：「代陂之役也。

translations.literal: ’ Those about said: ‘It is the affair of the Daipi battle.’
translations.idiomatic: His attendants said, ‘They mourn the dead of Daipi.’

sentences.zh: 」裒益慚恨。

translations.literal: ’ Pou increased in shame and resentment.
translations.idiomatic: The answer deepened his shame.

sentences.zh: 永和五年卒，年四十七，遠近嗟悼，吏士哀慕之。

translations.literal: In the fifth year of Yonghe he died, age forty-seven; far and near sighed and mourned; clerks and soldiers sorrowfully longed for him.
translations.idiomatic: He died in 349 at forty-seven; people everywhere grieved, and his troops mourned him bitterly.

sentences.zh: 贈侍中、太傅，本官如故，諡曰元穆。

translations.literal: He was posthumously awarded Palace Attendant and Grand Tutor; his original office was as before; his posthumous name was Yuanmu (‘Primordial Solemn’).
translations.idiomatic: He was posthumously named Palace Attendant and Grand Tutor, kept his military titles, and received the posthumous name Yuanmu.

sentences.zh: 子歆，字幼安，以學行知名，歷散騎常侍、秘書監。

translations.literal: His son Xin, styled You’an, was known for learning and conduct; he passed through Regular Cavalier Attendant and Director of the Palace Library.
translations.idiomatic: His son Chu Xin, courtesy name You’an, was known for scholarship and character and served as Regular Cavalier Attendant and director of the Palace Library.

sentences.zh: 惔官至南康太守，早卒。

translations.literal: Tan rose to Administrator of Nankang and died early.
translations.idiomatic: Chu Tan became Administrator of Nankang but died young.

sentences.zh: 惔子元度，西陽太守；

translations.literal: Tan’s son Yuandu was Administrator of Xiyang;
translations.idiomatic: Chu Tan’s son Yuandu was Administrator of Xiyang;

sentences.zh: 次叔度，太常卿、尚書。

translations.literal: next Shudu was Minister of the Grand Temple and Director.
translations.idiomatic: his younger brother Shudu rose to Minister of the Grand Temple and director in the Department of State Affairs.

sentences.zh: 澄字季玄，起家秘書郎，轉丞，清正有器望，累遷秘書監、太常、中護軍。

translations.literal: Cheng styled Jixuan, from family rise was Palace Library gentleman, transferred to assistant director; clear and upright he had vessel and repute; he was repeatedly promoted to Director of the Palace Library, Minister of the Grand Temple, and Central Protector of the Army.
translations.idiomatic: Chu Cheng, courtesy name Jixuan, entered service as a secretary in the Palace Library, became assistant director, and rose on a reputation for integrity to director of the library, Minister of the Grand Temple, and Central Protector of the Army.

sentences.zh: 孝武帝深愛之，以為冠軍將軍、吳國內史。

translations.literal: Emperor Xiaowu deeply loved him, making him Champion General and interior secretary of Wu.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Xiaowu favored him greatly and named him Champion General and interior secretary of the Wu princedom.

sentences.zh: 太元末，琅邪王出居外第，妙選師傅，徵拜尚書，領琅邪王師。

translations.literal: Near the end of Taiyuan, the Prince of Langye went out to dwell in an outer mansion; with subtle selection of tutor and mentor, he was summoned and appointed Director, concurrent tutor to the Prince of Langye.
translations.idiomatic: Late in Taiyuan, when the Prince of Langye moved to an outside residence, Chu Cheng was chosen as his tutor, recalled as a director in the Department of State Affairs, and named preceptor to the prince.

sentences.zh: 安帝即位，遷尚書左僕射，典選、王師如故。

translations.literal: When Emperor An ascended the throne, he was promoted to Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, directing selection, tutor to the prince as before.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor An he became Left Vice Director, kept charge of appointments, and remained the prince’s tutor.

sentences.zh: 時澄腳疾，固讓，特聽不朝，坐家視事。

translations.literal: At the time Cheng had foot ailment, firmly declined, was specially permitted not to attend court, and sat at home overseeing affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Crippled by foot trouble, he begged off court audiences and was allowed to manage business from home.

sentences.zh: 又領本州大中正。

translations.literal: Further he held concurrent great rectifier of his native province.
translations.idiomatic: He also served as senior rectifier for his home province.

sentences.zh: 及桓玄執政，以疾奏免，卒於家。

translations.literal: When Huan Xuan grasped government, on account of illness he was memorialized dismissed; he died at home.
translations.idiomatic: When Huan Xuan took power, Chu Cheng was removed on grounds of illness and died at home.

sentences.zh: 安帝反正，追贈金紫光祿大夫。

translations.literal: When Emperor An returned to right, he was posthumously awarded Grand Master of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.
translations.idiomatic: After Emperor An’s restoration he was posthumously named Grand Master of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.

sentences.zh: 長子籍，早卒。

translations.literal: His eldest son Ji died early.
translations.idiomatic: His eldest son Chu Ji died young.

sentences.zh: 次子融，元熙中，為大司農。

translations.literal: His second son Rong, in the Yuanxi period, was Grand Minister of Agriculture.
translations.idiomatic: His second son Chu Rong became Grand Minister of Agriculture under Yuanxi.

sentences.zh: 王濛，字仲祖，哀靖皇后父也。

translations.literal: Wang Meng, styled Zhongzu, was the father of Empress Aijing.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Meng, courtesy name Zhongzu, was the father of Empress Aijing.

sentences.zh: 曾祖黯，歷位尚書。

translations.literal: His great-grandfather An passed through posts to Director.
translations.idiomatic: His great-grandfather Wang An had served as a director in the Department of State Affairs.

sentences.zh: 祖佑，北軍中候。

translations.literal: His grandfather You was Commandant of the Northern Army.
translations.idiomatic: His grandfather Wang You was commandant of the Northern Army.

sentences.zh: 父訥，新淦令。

translations.literal: His father Ne was magistrate of Xingan.
translations.idiomatic: His father Wang Ne was magistrate of Xingan.

sentences.zh: 濛少時放縱不羈，不為鄉曲所齒，晚節始克己勵行，有風流美譽，虛己應物，恕而後行，莫不敬愛焉。

translations.literal: Meng in youth was unrestrained and not bound, not ranked by local society; in late integrity he first restrained self and urged conduct, had elegant repute, emptied self in responding to things, forgave and afterward acted—none did not revere and love him.
translations.idiomatic: In youth Wang Meng was a wild rake whom neighbors scorned; in maturity he disciplined himself, won a name for grace and charm, met the world with humility, and acted only after forgiving others—everyone then esteemed him.

sentences.zh: 事諸母甚謹，奉祿資產常推厚居薄，喜慍不形於色，不修小潔，而以清約見稱。

translations.literal: Serving his various mothers he was very careful; in salary and assets he always pushed thick and dwelt thin; joy and anger did not show on his face; he did not cultivate petty purity, but by clarity and abstemiousness was praised.
translations.idiomatic: He treated his stepmothers with great care, kept the better share of income for them while living modestly himself, hid his feelings, cared little for petty scruples, and was admired for frugal simplicity.

sentences.zh: 善隸書。

translations.literal: He was good at clerical script.
translations.idiomatic: He excelled at clerical calligraphy.

sentences.zh: 美姿容，嘗覽鏡自照，稱其父字曰：「王文開生如此兒邪！

translations.literal: Handsome in bearing, he once looked in a mirror and shone on himself, calling his father’s style: ‘Did Wang Wenkai sire such a son!’
translations.idiomatic: Handsome enough to admire himself in the mirror, he would joke using his father’s style name, ‘Could Wang Wenkai really have fathered a son like this?’

sentences.zh: 」居貧，帽敗，自入市買之，嫗悅其貌，遺以新帽，時人以為達。

translations.literal: ’ Dwelling in poverty, his cap was ruined; he himself entered the market to buy one; an old woman delighted in his looks and gave him a new cap; people of the time thought him comprehending.
translations.idiomatic: Poor and needing a new hat, he went to market; an old woman smitten with his looks gave him one, and contemporaries praised his easy unconcern.

sentences.zh: 與沛國劉惔齊名友善，惔常稱濛性至通，而自然有節，濛每云：「劉君知我，勝我自知。

translations.literal: With Liu Tan of Pei he shared fame and friendship; Tan often praised Meng’s nature as supremely penetrating, yet naturally having restraint; Meng always said: ‘Lord Liu knows me better than I know myself.’
translations.idiomatic: He and Liu Tan of Pei were close and equally celebrated. Liu Tan said Wang Meng combined perfect ease with natural restraint; Wang Meng said, ‘Liu understands me better than I do myself.’

sentences.zh: 」時人以惔方荀奉倩，濛比袁曜卿，凡稱風流者，舉濛、惔為宗焉。

translations.literal: ’ People of the time paired Tan with Xun Fengqian and compared Meng to Yuan Yaoqing; whenever speaking of elegant bearing, they raised Meng and Tan as the masters.
translations.idiomatic: Critics likened Liu Tan to Xun Can and Wang Meng to Yuan Yao; anyone discussing ‘refined spirit’ took the pair as the standard.

sentences.zh: 司徒王導辟為掾。

translations.literal: Minister of Education Wang Dao summoned him as clerk.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dao, minister of education, recruited him for his staff.

sentences.zh: 導復引匡術弟孝，濛致箋於導曰：「開國承家，小人勿用。

translations.literal: Dao again brought in Kuang Shu’s younger brother Xiao; Meng sent a note to Dao saying: ‘Founding the state and inheriting the house—petty men are not to be used.’
translations.idiomatic: When Wang Dao also employed Xiao, brother of Kuang Shu, Wang Meng wrote, ‘The Book of Changes warns: when founding a dynasty and family, do not employ petty men.’

sentences.zh: 杖德義以尹天下，方將澄清彝倫，崇重名器。

translations.literal: Relying on virtue and rightness to govern the world, you are about to clarify the constant norms and honor heavy titles and vessels.
translations.idiomatic: You propose to govern by moral authority, restore ethical order, and elevate the institutions of state.

sentences.zh: 夫軍國殊用，文武異容，豈可令涇渭混流，虧清穆之風，以允答具瞻，儀形海內！

translations.literal: Now army and state have distinct uses, civil and martial different bearing—how can you let the Jing and Wei rivers mix in flow, injuring the wind of pure solemnity, thereby answering the gathered gaze and modeling form within the seas!
translations.idiomatic: Military and civil service are not the same; how can you muddy the clear distinction and spoil the court’s grave dignity before a watching empire?

sentences.zh: 」導不答。

translations.literal: ’ Dao did not reply.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Dao did not answer.

sentences.zh: 後出補長山令，復為司徒左西屬。

translations.literal: Afterward he went out to fill Changshan magistrate, and again became the Minister of Education’s left western subordinate.
translations.idiomatic: He later became magistrate of Changshan, then returned to the capital as a senior clerk on Wang Dao’s staff.

sentences.zh: 濛以此職有譴則應受杖，固辭。

translations.literal: Meng held that this office, if there were fault, should receive beating; he firmly declined.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Meng refused the post because its holders could be flogged for mistakes.

sentences.zh: 詔為停罰，猶不就。

translations.literal: An edict for him suspended punishment; still he did not take it.
translations.idiomatic: The throne waived corporal punishment for him, but he still would not serve.

sentences.zh: 徙中書郎。

translations.literal: He was transferred to gentleman of the Palace Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: He was moved to a post as gentleman of the Palace Secretariat.

sentences.zh: 簡文帝之為會稽王也，嘗與孫綽商略諸風流人，綽言曰：「劉惔清蔚簡令，王濛溫潤恬和，桓溫高爽邁出。

translations.literal: When Emperor Jianwen was Prince of Kuaiji, he once with Sun Chuo discussed and surveyed the various men of elegant bearing; Chuo spoke, saying: ‘Liu Tan is clear, lush, terse, and fine; Wang Meng is warm, moist, quiet, and mild; Huan Wen is lofty, bright, and strides beyond.’
translations.idiomatic: While still Prince of Kuaiji, Emperor Jianwen once asked Sun Chuo to rank the leading gentlemen. Sun Chuo said, ‘Liu Tan is spare and luminous; Wang Meng is gentle and serene; Huan Wen is bold and towering.’

sentences.zh: 謝尚清易令達，而濛性和暢，能言理，辭簡而有會。

translations.literal: Xie Shang is clear, easy, fine, and penetrating; but Meng’s nature is harmonious and smooth, able to speak principle, phrasing terse yet having convergence.’
translations.idiomatic: Xie Shang is lucid and open; Wang Meng’s temper is even, he reasons well, and his words are brief but hit the mark.’

sentences.zh: 」及簡文帝輔政，益貴幸之，與劉惔號為入室之賓。

translations.literal: ’ When Emperor Jianwen assisted governance, he increasingly honored and favored him; with Liu Tan he was styled guests who entered the inner chamber.
translations.idiomatic: When the prince became regent, Wang Meng grew ever closer to him; he and Liu Tan were called intimates who might enter the inner rooms.

sentences.zh: 轉司徒左長史。

translations.literal: He was transferred to senior clerk on the left of the Minister of Education.
translations.idiomatic: He was promoted to senior clerk on Wang Dao’s left.

sentences.zh: 晚求為東陽，不許。

translations.literal: In late years he sought to be Dongyang; it was not permitted.
translations.idiomatic: Late in life he asked to be sent to Dongyang; the court refused.

sentences.zh: 及濛病，乃恨不用之。

translations.literal: When Meng fell ill, then he regretted not having used him.
translations.idiomatic: Only when Wang Meng fell ill did the prince regret not granting his request.

sentences.zh: 濛聞之曰：「人言會稽王癡，竟癡也！

translations.literal: Meng heard it and said: ‘People say the Prince of Kuaiji is dull—he really is dull!’
translations.idiomatic: Wang Meng heard and said, ‘They call the Prince of Kuaiji slow-witted—they are right!’

sentences.zh: 」疾漸篤，於燈下轉麈尾視之，歎曰：「如此人曾不得四十也！

translations.literal: ’ His illness gradually grew grave; under the lamp he turned a yak-tail chowry and looked at it, sighing: ‘Such a man could not even reach forty!’
translations.idiomatic: As his illness worsened, he turned his fly-whisk in the lamplight and sighed, ‘A man like me will not see forty.’

sentences.zh: 」年三十九卒。

translations.literal: ’ At age thirty-nine he died.
translations.idiomatic: He died at thirty-nine.

sentences.zh: 臨殯，劉惔以犀杷麈尾置棺中，因慟絕久之。

translations.literal: At the laying-in for burial, Liu Tan with a rhinoceros-ivory handle placed a yak-tail chowry in the coffin; thereupon he wailed and fainted for a long time.
translations.idiomatic: At the funeral Liu Tan laid a rhinoceros-handled fly-whisk in the coffin and sobbed until he collapsed.

sentences.zh: 謝安亦常稱濛云：「王長史語甚不多，可謂有令音。

translations.literal: Xie An also often praised Meng, saying: ‘Chief Clerk Wang’s words are very few; one may say he has a fine tone.’
translations.idiomatic: Xie An used to say of him, ‘Chief Clerk Wang spoke little, but every word rang true.’

sentences.zh: 」有二子：修、蘊。

translations.literal: ’ He had two sons: Xiu and Yun.
translations.idiomatic: He had two sons, Wang Xiu and Wang Yun.

sentences.zh: 修字敬仁，小字苟子。

translations.literal: Xiu styled Jingren, childhood name Gouzi.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Xiu, courtesy name Jingren, was called Gouzi in childhood.

sentences.zh: 明秀有美稱，善隸書，號曰流奕清舉。

translations.literal: Bright and elegant, he had a fine reputation; he was good at clerical script, titled Flowing Brightness, Clear Uplift.
translations.idiomatic: Brilliant and admired, he excelled at clerical script in a style praised as fluid, lucid, and lifted.

sentences.zh: 年十二，作《賢全論》。

translations.literal: At age twelve, he composed ‘Treatise on Worthy Wholeness.’
translations.idiomatic: At twelve he wrote the Treatise on Worthy Wholeness.

sentences.zh: 濛以示劉惔曰：「敬仁此論，便足以參微言。

translations.literal: Meng showed it to Liu Tan, saying: ‘Jingren’s treatise is enough to join subtle words.’
translations.idiomatic: Wang Meng showed it to Liu Tan and said, ‘Jingren’s essay already touches the subtlest teachings.’

sentences.zh: 」起家著作郎、琅邪王文學，轉中軍司馬，未拜而卒，年二十四。

translations.literal: ’ From family rise he was editorial director and literary instructor to the Prince of Langye, transferred to army major under the Central Army; before taking office he died, age twenty-four.
translations.idiomatic: He began as editorial director and tutor to the Prince of Langye, then was named major on the central army staff but died before assuming duty, at twenty-four.

sentences.zh: 臨終，歎曰：「無愧古人，年與之齊矣。」

translations.literal: Facing the end, he sighed, saying: ‘I have no shame before the ancients; my years match theirs.’
translations.idiomatic: On his deathbed he said, ‘I need not blush before the ancients—I have lived as long as many of them.’

sentences.zh: 王遐，字桓子，簡順皇后父，驃騎將軍述之從叔也。

translations.literal: Wang Xia, styled Huanzi, was the father of Empress Jianshun, paternal uncle’s son to Grand General Who Gallops as if Flying Shu.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Xia, courtesy name Huanzi, father of Empress Jianshun, was a cousin of Wang Shu, Grand General Who Gallops as if Flying.

sentences.zh: 少以華族，仕至光祿勳。

translations.literal: In youth by splendid clan, he served to Supervisor of the Household.
translations.idiomatic: Born to a great house, he rose to Supervisor of the Household.

sentences.zh: 甯康初，追贈特進、光祿大夫，加散騎常侍，諡曰靖。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Ningkang, he was posthumously awarded Exalted Marcher, Grand Master of Splendid Carriage, added as Regular Cavalier Attendant; his posthumous name was Jing (‘Tranquil’).
translations.idiomatic: Early in Ningkang he was posthumously honored as Exalted Marcher and Grand Master of Splendid Carriage with Regular Cavalier Attendant, posthumous name Jing.

sentences.zh: 長子恪，領軍將軍。

translations.literal: His eldest son Ke was General Who Commands the Army.
translations.idiomatic: His eldest son Wang Ke became General Who Commands the Army.

sentences.zh: 恪子欣之，豫章太守，秩中二千石。

translations.literal: Ke’s son Xinzhi was Administrator of Yuzhang, salary at the two-thousand-shi middle grade.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Ke’s son Wang Xinzhi served as Administrator of Yuzhang at the two-thousand-shi rank.

sentences.zh: 欣之弟歡之，廣州刺史。

translations.literal: Xinzhi’s younger brother Huanzhi was Inspector of Guangzhou.
translations.idiomatic: His brother Wang Huanzhi became Inspector of Guangzhou.

sentences.zh: 遐少子臻，崇德衛尉。

translations.literal: Xia’s younger son Zhen was Commandant of the Guards of Chongde.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Xia’s youngest son Wang Zhen was Commandant of the Guards at Chongde.

sentences.zh: 王蘊，字叔仁，孝武定皇后父，司徒左長史濛之子也。

translations.literal: Wang Yun, styled Shuren, was the father of Empress Xiaowu Ding, son of senior clerk on the left Meng.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Yun, courtesy name Shuren, father of Empress Xiaowu Ding, was the son of Wang Meng, senior clerk on the minister’s left.

sentences.zh: 起家佐著作郎，累遷尚書吏部郎。

translations.literal: From family rise he was assistant editorial director; he was repeatedly promoted to gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel in the Department of State Affairs.
translations.idiomatic: He began as assistant editorial director and rose to head of the personnel bureau in the Department of State Affairs.

sentences.zh: 性平和，不抑寒素，每一官缺，求者十輩，蘊無所是非。

translations.literal: By nature even and mild, he did not suppress the cold and plain; whenever one office was vacant, seekers were ten groups; Yun had no yes or no for them.
translations.idiomatic: Even-tempered, he did not slight men of humble origin; when a post opened and dozens applied, he refused to pick favorites in advance.

sentences.zh: 時簡文帝為會稽王，輔政，蘊輒連狀白之，曰：「某人有地，某人有才。

translations.literal: At the time Emperor Jianwen was Prince of Kuaiji, assisting governance; Yun always linked memorials and reported to him, saying: ‘So-and-so has pedigree; so-and-so has talent.’
translations.idiomatic: While the Prince of Kuaiji was regent, Wang Yun sent him lists: ‘This man has standing; that man has ability.’

sentences.zh: 」務存進達，各隨其方，故不得者無怨焉。

translations.literal: ’ He strove to preserve advancement and reaching, each following his direction; therefore those who did not obtain had no resentment.
translations.idiomatic: He pushed every candidate on his merits, so those passed over had no cause for bitterness.

sentences.zh: 補吳興太守，甚有德政。

translations.literal: He was appointed Administrator of Wuxing and had very virtuous governance.
translations.idiomatic: As Administrator of Wuxing he governed with conspicuous virtue.

sentences.zh: 屬郡荒人饑，輒開倉贍恤。

translations.literal: When the attached commandery was barren and people hungry, he always opened granaries to relieve and pity.
translations.idiomatic: When famine struck his jurisdiction, he opened the granaries without waiting for higher approval.

sentences.zh: 主簿執諫，請先列表上待報，蘊曰：「今百姓嗷然，路有饑饉，若表上須報，何以救將死之命乎！

translations.literal: The chief clerk firmly remonstrated, requesting first to list in a memorial upward and await reply; Yun said: ‘Now the hundred surnames cry out; on the roads there is starvation; if memorializing upward must await reply, how save lives about to die!’
translations.idiomatic: His chief clerk urged him to seek permission first. Wang Yun replied, ‘The people are starving in the streets; if we wait on paperwork, we let them die!’

sentences.zh: 專輒之愆，罪在太守，且行仁義而敗，無所恨也。

translations.literal: The fault of usurpation—guilt lies with the administrator; moreover, practicing benevolence and rightness yet failing, there is nothing to regret.’
translations.idiomatic: If acting on my own is a crime, blame the administrator; I would rather fail doing right than watch them perish.’

sentences.zh: 」於是大振貸之，賴蘊全者十七八焉。

translations.literal: ’ Thereupon he greatly extended loans to them; those who relied on Yun to be saved were seven or eight in ten.
translations.idiomatic: He distributed grain on a large scale; perhaps eight in ten survivors owed their lives to him.

sentences.zh: 朝廷以違科免蘊官，士庶詣闕訟之，詔特左降晉陵太守。

translations.literal: The court on account of violating statute dismissed Yun from office; gentry and commoners went to the gate to sue for him; an edict specially demoted him left to Administrator of Jinling.
translations.idiomatic: The court cashiered him for breaking regulations, but a popular petition at the palace gates won him a reduced sentence: demotion to Administrator of Jinling.

sentences.zh: 復有惠化，百姓歌之。

translations.literal: Again he had kindly transformation; the hundred surnames sang him.
translations.idiomatic: There too his benevolent rule won the people’s songs.

sentences.zh: 定后立，以后父，遷光祿大夫，領五兵尚書、本州大中正，封建昌縣侯。

translations.literal: When Empress Ding was established, on account of being the empress’s father, he was promoted to Grand Master of Splendid Carriage, concurrent Minister of the Five Armies, great rectifier of his native province, enfeoffed as Marquis of Jianchang County.
translations.idiomatic: When the Ding empress was enthroned, he became Grand Master of Splendid Carriage, minister of the Five Armies, senior rectifier for his province, and Marquis of Jianchang.

sentences.zh: 蘊以恩澤賜爵，非三代令典，固辭不受。

translations.literal: Yun held that enfeoffment by grace and favor was not the fine norm of the Three Dynasties; he firmly declined and did not accept.
translations.idiomatic: He argued that a title won only through imperial favor was not like the old canonical grants and refused it.

sentences.zh: 朝廷敦勸，終不肯拜，乃授都督京口諸軍事、左將軍、徐州刺史、假節，復固讓。

translations.literal: The court earnestly urged; in the end he would not take office; thereupon he was awarded military overseer of Jingkou affairs, General of the Left, Inspector of Xuzhou, with credentials; again he firmly declined.
translations.idiomatic: Despite repeated pressure he would not accept the marquisate, so they named him commander at Jingkou, General of the Left, and Inspector of Xuzhou with credentials—which he also tried to refuse.

sentences.zh: 謝安謂蘊曰：「卿居后父之重，不應妄自菲薄，以虧時遇，宜依褚公故事，但令在貴權於事不事耳。

translations.literal: Xie An said to Yun: ‘You occupy the weight of the empress’s father; you ought not lightly belittle yourself, thereby injuring timely encounter; you should follow Lord Chu’s precedent, only letting him dwell in honor and power, in affairs not handling affairs.’
translations.idiomatic: Xie An told him, ‘As the empress’s father you must not sell yourself short. Do as Chu Pou did: take the high title but leave day-to-day duties to others.’

sentences.zh: 可暫臨此任，以紓國姻之重。

translations.literal: You may for a time take this post, thereby easing the weight of the state’s marriage tie.’
translations.idiomatic: Take the post for now to satisfy the court’s need to honor the imperial marriage.’

sentences.zh: 」於是乃受命，鎮於京口。

translations.literal: ’ Thereupon he then accepted the command and garrisoned at Jingkou.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Yun then took command and stationed his headquarters at Jingkou.

sentences.zh: 頃之，徵拜尚書左僕射，將軍如故，遷丹陽尹，即本軍號加散騎常侍。

translations.literal: In a short while, he was summoned and appointed Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, general as before, promoted to Intendant of Danyang, on his original army title adding Regular Cavalier Attendant.
